questions.stem: The NOBEL PRIZE was instituted in the WILL of Swedish industrialist ALFRED NOBEL, inventor of:
questions.explanation: ALFRED BERNHARD NOBEL (1833-1896) — Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman; best known for INVENTING DYNAMITE (patented 1867) — a safer formulation of NITROGLYCERIN (a violently unstable liquid explosive discovered by Italian Sobrero, 1847) absorbed onto DIATOMACEOUS EARTH (kieselguhr), making it stable enough to transport + use in construction, mining, tunnelling, demolition. BUSINESS: founded BOFORS (armaments firm, Sweden) + 90 factories in 20 countries; developed ballistite (smokeless powder). Personal tragedy: his brother Emil was killed in a nitroglycerin explosion at Nobel's factory (1864), which spurred him to make it safer. WILL: Drafted on 27 November 1895, a year before his death. When he died in San Remo, Italy, 10 December 1896 (age 63), no direct heirs; 94% of his assets were directed to fund FIVE PRIZES for those who had ‘conferred the greatest benefit on mankind’. Why? Legend: In 1888, his brother Ludvig died; a French newspaper erroneously wrote an obituary of Alfred titled ‘Le marchand de la mort est mort’ (‘The merchant of death is dead’), criticising him for his inventions. Shocked at how he would be remembered, he determined to reshape his legacy — hence the PEACE prize and the others. THE ORIGINAL FIVE NOBEL PRIZES (first awarded 1901): (1) PHYSICS — awarded by Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences; (2) CHEMISTRY — same; (3) PHYSIOLOGY OR MEDICINE — Karolinska Institute; (4) LITERATURE — Swedish Academy; (5) PEACE — Norwegian Nobel Committee (at the time Sweden + Norway were in union; after 1905 separation, Norway retained this role per Nobel's will). SIXTH PRIZE — NOBEL MEMORIAL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES, instituted 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank (Swedish Central Bank) in memory of Nobel, on its 300th anniversary; FIRST AWARDED 1969 (to Ragnar Frisch + Jan Tinbergen). TECHNICALLY not a Nobel Prize per se but administered identically. PRIZE CEREMONY: annually on 10 DECEMBER (Nobel's death anniversary) — Peace Prize in OSLO, others in STOCKHOLM. Each laureate receives a gold medal + diploma + cash award (currently ~11 million Swedish Kronor, ~$1 million). Max 3 laureates per prize per year. Prize can NOT be awarded posthumously (rule since 1974), EXCEPT if laureate dies between announcement + ceremony; ONE exception (Ralph Steinman, Medicine 2011 — died 3 days before announcement, committee didn't know, decision stood). patented 1867; a safe-to-handle formulation of nitroglycerin absorbed on diatomaceous earth; Nobel's will (1895) set aside his fortune (~$265 mn in 2024 $) to endow the Prizes.

questions.stem: The FIRST INDIAN to win a NOBEL PRIZE was:

options.option_text: RABINDRANATH TAGORE — NOBEL PRIZE IN LITERATURE 1913, for his work ‘GITANJALI’ (Song Offerings) — also the first NON-EUROPEAN to win this prize

questions.explanation: RABINDRANATH TAGORE (1861-1941) — Bengali polymath; poet, philosopher, musician, painter, educationist, novelist, playwright, social reformer. WON the NOBEL PRIZE IN LITERATURE 1913 — ‘because of his profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse, by which, with consummate skill, he has made his poetic thought, expressed in his own English words, a part of the literature of the West’. FIRST INDIAN + FIRST NON-EUROPEAN + FIRST ASIAN to win the Nobel Prize. Awarded for his work ‘GITANJALI’ (Song Offerings) — English translation (by himself) of his Bengali devotional poems, published 1910-12 in Bengali, 1912 in English with an introduction by W.B. YEATS. OTHER ACHIEVEMENTS of Tagore: (1) Founded SHANTINIKETAN (1901, in Bolpur, Birbhum district, West Bengal) — experimental school emphasizing open-air learning, synthesis of East-West; grew into VISHVA-BHARATI UNIVERSITY (1921, central university since 1951). (2) Composed INDIA'S NATIONAL ANTHEM ‘JANA GANA MANA’ (first sung 1911, Calcutta Congress session; adopted 24 Jan 1950). (3) Composed BANGLADESH'S NATIONAL ANTHEM ‘AMAR SHONAR BANGLA’ (1905, during Bengal partition protest; adopted 1971). (4) Influenced SRI LANKA'S national anthem ‘Sri Lanka Matha’ (written by his student Ananda Samarakoon). (5) RETURNED KNIGHTHOOD (‘Sir’, given by British 1915) in 1919 to PROTEST the JALLIANWALA BAGH MASSACRE. (6) Travelled extensively — friendship with Einstein (famous dialogue on science + mysticism), Yeats, Ezra Pound, Gandhi (called Tagore ‘Gurudev’). (7) KEY WORKS: Poetry — Gitanjali, Gitimalya, Balaka, Puravi, Sanchaita. Novels — Chokher Bali, Gora, Ghare Baire (The Home and The World — film by Satyajit Ray 1984), Chaturanga, Shesher Kobita. Drama — Dak Ghar, Raja, Muktadhara, Rakta Karabi. Short stories — Kabuliwallah, Postmaster. Essays — Sadhana, Creative Unity, Personality. (8) RABINDRA SANGEET — 2,000+ songs; a distinct musical tradition. (9) PAINTER — began at 60, over 2,000 works, modernist style. (10) JAMINI ROY, NANDALAL BOSE were among his students. INDIAN / INDIAN-ORIGIN NOBEL LAUREATES to date (chronological): (1) TAGORE — Literature 1913; (2) C.V. RAMAN — Physics 1930 (Raman effect, scattering of light — only Indian Physics Nobel); (3) HARGOBIND KHORANA — Medicine 1968 (genetic code/RNA synthesis — Indian-born, US citizen); (4) MOTHER TERESA — Peace 1979 (humanitarian work in Kolkata — born in Albania, Indian citizen); (5) SUBRAHMANYAN CHANDRASEKHAR — Physics 1983 (stellar structure, Chandrasekhar limit — nephew of CV Raman, Indian-born US citizen); (6) AMARTYA SEN — Economics 1998 (welfare economics, famines — born Bengal, mostly UK); (7) V. RAMAKRISHNAN — Chemistry 2009 (ribosome structure — born TN, US+UK citizen); (8) KAILASH SATYARTHI — Peace 2014 (with Malala Yousafzai, children's rights, Bachpan Bachao Andolan); (9) ABHIJIT VINAYAK BANERJEE — Economics 2019 (with Esther Duflo + Michael Kremer, poverty alleviation experimental approach — Indian-American). So, TWO resident-Indian-citizen Nobels: C.V. Raman, Kailash Satyarthi; others were Indian-born naturalised citizens of other countries.

questions.stem: C.V. RAMAN won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for:
questions.explanation: SIR CHANDRASEKHARA VENKATA RAMAN (1888-1970) — Indian physicist; born Tiruchirappalli, TN; FIRST ASIAN + first NON-WHITE to win Nobel Prize in a SCIENCE discipline. NOBEL PRIZE IN PHYSICS 1930 — ‘for his work on the SCATTERING OF LIGHT and for the discovery of the effect named after him’. THE RAMAN EFFECT — discovered on 28 FEBRUARY 1928 at Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS), Calcutta/Kolkata. DAY celebrated as NATIONAL SCIENCE DAY in India. DESCRIPTION: when monochromatic light passes through a transparent medium (gas, liquid, or solid), a TINY FRACTION (~1 in a million photons) of the scattered light has a DIFFERENT WAVELENGTH from the incident light — due to INELASTIC scattering in which the photon exchanges energy with the molecule's VIBRATIONAL or ROTATIONAL modes. The shifted wavelengths (Stokes + anti-Stokes lines) form the ‘RAMAN SPECTRUM’, unique to each molecule — like a molecular FINGERPRINT. Applications: (1) CHEMICAL ANALYSIS — identify substances non-destructively; (2) MATERIALS SCIENCE — graphene, semiconductor quality; (3) PHARMACEUTICALS — purity, counterfeit detection; (4) ART CONSERVATION — pigment identification; (5) SECURITY SCREENING — detect explosives/narcotics; (6) EARTH + PLANETARY SCIENCES — MARS rovers (Perseverance has SHERLOC instrument using Raman); (7) MEDICAL DIAGNOSTICS — tumour identification. CONTEXT OF DISCOVERY: Raman, returning by ship from London in 1921, was intrigued by the BLUE OF THE MEDITERRANEAN; Lord Rayleigh's explanation of blue sky (Rayleigh scattering) didn't fully satisfy him regarding the sea — a different kind of scattering seemed involved. Back in Calcutta, he + K.S. Krishnan worked with meticulous spectroscopy on various liquids (benzene, etc.) and isolated the shifted lines in scattered light. Used merely a MERCURY ARC LAMP + PRISM + SPECTROSCOPE — a triumph of Indian indigenous science with modest equipment. Simultaneously + independently, Soviet scientists LANDSBERG + MANDELSTAM discovered the same in 1928 in crystals, but Raman's publication was earlier (31 March 1928, Nature journal). HONORS: Knighthood (Sir, 1929); BHARAT RATNA (1954 — the FIRST awarded, along with Rajaji + Radhakrishnan); Lenin Peace Prize (1957). FOUNDED: Indian Academy of Sciences (Bengaluru, 1934); Raman Research Institute (Bengaluru, 1948). STUDENTS: S. CHANDRASEKHAR (nephew, Nobel 1983 — stellar structure, black holes), HOMI BHABHA (father of Indian atomic programme, though not a direct PhD student — met at Raman's institute). KEY LESSON: Raman rejected JOB OFFERS from UK/US; chose to do cutting-edge physics IN INDIA + with Indian institutional support — a symbol of Indian scientific self-reliance. the inelastic scattering of light by molecules, which reveals molecular vibrational modes; discovered 28 February 1928; announced in ‘Nature’ + ‘Indian Journal of Physics’.

questions.stem: The NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 was shared by Kailash Satyarthi and:
questions.explanation: NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 — jointly awarded to KAILASH SATYARTHI (Indian, b. 11 Jan 1954, Vidisha, MP) and MALALA YOUSAFZAI (Pakistani, b. 12 July 1997, Mingora, Swat Valley) — ‘for their struggle against the suppression of children and young people and for the right of all children to education’. Malala (at 17) became the YOUNGEST-EVER NOBEL LAUREATE in any category. This joint award of an Indian + Pakistani — Hindu + Muslim — was SYMBOLIC, urging peace across the subcontinent. KAILASH SATYARTHI: (1) Founded BACHPAN BACHAO ANDOLAN (BBA, ‘Save the Childhood Movement’) in 1980, rescuing children from bonded labour + trafficking in India; liberated >85,000 children. (2) Initiated GLOBAL MARCH AGAINST CHILD LABOUR (1998) — 80,000-km march across 103 countries — led to ILO Convention 182 on WORST FORMS OF CHILD LABOUR (1999, most rapidly ratified convention in ILO history). (3) RugMark (now GoodWeave) — certification of child-labour-free carpets. (4) Padma Shri awarded 2025 (not before; he had refused earlier honours while children were still in bondage, per one account). Several other Indian honours. (5) Post-Nobel: expanded to 100 Million for 100 Million Campaign (youth global action for marginalised children); Laureates & Leaders for Children; led Fair Share for Children Fund. MALALA YOUSAFZAI: (1) Daughter of education activist Ziauddin; blogged anonymously for BBC Urdu from age 11 about Taliban's ban on girls' schools in Swat valley. (2) Survived an assassination attempt by Taliban: on 9 OCT 2012, a Taliban gunman boarded her school bus and shot her in the head at close range. Airlifted first to Peshawar, then Birmingham UK for brain surgery. Miraculously survived + became a global symbol. (3) ‘I AM MALALA’ (2013, autobiography co-authored with Christina Lamb) — international bestseller, translated to many languages. (4) Founded MALALA FUND for girls' education worldwide. (5) Graduated from OXFORD (Lady Margaret Hall, PPE, 2020). (6) 2013 Sakharov Prize; 2013 Pakistani youth peace prize; UN honorary Messenger of Peace. MALALA DAY — 12 July (her birthday), declared by UN since 2013. OTHER famous PEACE NOBEL LAUREATES: Henri Dunant (1901, 1st — Red Cross founder), Theodore Roosevelt (1906, Russo-Japan peace), Albert Schweitzer (1952), Martin Luther King Jr (1964), Willy Brandt (1971, Ostpolitik), Dalai Lama (1989), Nelson Mandela + F.W. de Klerk (1993), Yitzhak Rabin + Shimon Peres + Yasser Arafat (1994, Oslo Accords), Aung San Suu Kyi (1991 — later controversial over Rohingya), Barack Obama (2009 — controversial), Muhammad Yunus + Grameen Bank (2006, microfinance), Mother Teresa (1979 — 1st India-based), AL Gore + IPCC (2007, climate). 2024: NIHON HIDANKYO (Japanese atomic bomb survivors org). 2025: MARIA CORINA MACHADO (Venezuelan opposition leader). Pakistani activist for girls' education; at 17, the YOUNGEST EVER Nobel Laureate; shot by the Taliban in 2012 for advocating girls' schooling.

questions.stem: AMARTYA SEN won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences 1998 for his contributions to:
questions.explanation: AMARTYA KUMAR SEN (b. 3 Nov 1933, Santiniketan, West Bengal) — Indian economist-philosopher. NOBEL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES 1998 ‘for his contributions to WELFARE ECONOMICS’ — specifically (1) SOCIAL CHOICE THEORY (axiomatic analysis of collective decision-making), (2) POVERTY + INEQUALITY INDICES (Sen index for poverty), (3) CAPABILITY APPROACH (human well-being measured by what people can DO and BE — capabilities — not just income), (4) analysis of famines demolishing myths. Sen was the FIRST ASIAN Nobel laureate in Economics. KEY CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) ‘POVERTY AND FAMINES: AN ESSAY ON ENTITLEMENT AND DEPRIVATION’ (1981) — LANDMARK book showing that famines are NOT caused solely by drops in food availability. The 1943 BENGAL FAMINE killed ~3 million Indians even though food output was HIGHER than in non-famine years; the problem was collapse of ENTITLEMENTS of certain groups (fishermen, weavers, peasant labourers) — inability to command food due to inflation, lack of work, administrative failures. FAMINE in a democracy — Sen argued — doesn't happen because free press + elections force action; ‘no famine has ever occurred in a functioning democracy’ (with free press). (2) ‘SOCIAL CHOICE THEORY’ — built on Kenneth Arrow's impossibility theorem; Sen's 1970 book ‘COLLECTIVE CHOICE AND SOCIAL WELFARE’ (expanded edition 2017). Developed Sen-Debreu criterion, Arrow-Sen theorem. (3) CAPABILITY APPROACH — co-developed with Martha Nussbaum; emphasises freedom to achieve well-being rather than utility/income alone; influenced HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI, UNDP 1990) that Sen co-designed with PAKISTANI ECONOMIST MAHBUB UL HAQ. HDI has 3 components: (a) Life expectancy, (b) Education (mean + expected years of schooling), (c) GNI per capita. (4) ‘THE ARGUMENTATIVE INDIAN’ (2005), ‘IDEA OF JUSTICE’ (2009) — philosophical books; argues for pluralistic tradition in India; departs from Rawls's justice-as-fairness in favour of comparative justice. LIFE: Born in Santiniketan founded by his grandfather's friend TAGORE; name ‘Amartya’ given by Tagore himself. Witness to 1943 Bengal famine as a child — shaped his life's work. Schooling at Shantiniketan's Patha Bhavana; BA Presidency College Calcutta; PhD from Trinity College, Cambridge. Taught at Delhi School of Economics, Trinity College Cambridge (Master 1998-2004), All Souls Oxford, LSE, Harvard. Currently Thomas W. Lamont University Professor, Harvard. AWARDS: BHARAT RATNA (1999); Padma Vibhushan; Padma Bhushan; National Humanities Medal (US 2011). Three wives including historian Emma Rothschild. CRITIQUES on policy: argued against Bangladesh-India-Pakistan spending too much on military; supported UPA's MGNREGA + Right to Food Act. PROBIR CHAKRAVARTY, JEAN DRÈZE (Belgian-Indian, long-time collaborator) — joint books: INDIA: ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND SOCIAL OPPORTUNITY (1995), AN UNCERTAIN GLORY: INDIA AND ITS CONTRADICTIONS (2013). OTHER INDIAN ECONOMICS Nobel: Abhijit Banerjee (2019, with wife Esther Duflo + Michael Kremer, for randomised controlled trials / RCTs in development economics; Indian-American; Presidency College + JNU + Harvard alumni). theory of social choice, poverty + famine analysis; showed famines are rarely due to absolute food shortage but to lack of entitlements (1981 book ‘Poverty and Famines’); co-developed HDI.

questions.stem: MOTHER TERESA was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in:
questions.explanation: MOTHER TERESA (1910-1997) — born ANJEZË GONXHE BOJAXHIU in SKOPJE, NORTH MACEDONIA (then Ottoman Empire, later Yugoslavia); of ALBANIAN ethnicity. Entered the LORETO sisters (Irish Catholic order) at 18, arrived in DARJEELING 1929, took final vows 1937 as ‘Sister Teresa’ (after Thérèse of Lisieux). Taught at St. Mary's school, Kolkata (1931-48), rising to principal. 1946 CALL WITHIN A CALL: on train journey Kolkata to Darjeeling (10 Sept, celebrated annually as INSPIRATION DAY), she felt a divine calling to leave her convent and serve the poorest of the poor. Permission granted 1948 by Vatican. Trained as nurse in Patna (with Medical Mission Sisters); returned to Kolkata, began serving destitute in slums of Motijheel. 1950 — FOUNDED MISSIONARIES OF CHARITY (Kolkata), initially 12 members, now 5,500+ sisters in 139 countries. Iconic WHITE SARI with three BLUE STRIPES became order's uniform. Adopted INDIAN CITIZENSHIP in 1948. Opened NIRMAL HRIDAY (Home for the Dying Destitutes) at Kalighat 1952, NIRMALA SHISHU BHAVAN (children), SHANTI NAGAR (leprosarium, Asansol), SHISHU BHAVAN, Titagarh leprosy centre, homes for AIDS patients, orphans globally. AWARDS: (1) PADMA SHRI 1962; (2) Jawaharlal Nehru Award for International Understanding 1969; (3) POPE John XXIII Peace Prize 1971; (4) BHARAT RATNA 1980 (first NATURALISED INDIAN citizen to receive it); (5) NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 1979 (gave her prize money to the poor; refused the ceremonial Nobel banquet + asked them to donate the banquet cost to the poor, $192,000 raised). (6) PRESIDENTIAL MEDAL OF FREEDOM (USA, 1985); (7) HONORARY CITIZENSHIP of USA (1996, only 6 persons ever). BEATIFIED 2003 by Pope John Paul II — ‘BLESSED TERESA OF CALCUTTA’. CANONIZED (made Saint) 4 September 2016 by Pope Francis — ‘SAINT TERESA OF CALCUTTA’. Her FEAST DAY: 5 September (death date). DEATH: 5 September 1997, Kolkata, aged 87. State funeral; her body lies in the Motherhouse of Missionaries of Charity, 54A Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Road, Kolkata — a pilgrimage site. CRITICS: (a) Christopher Hitchens's book ‘The Missionary Position’ (1995) alleged inadequate medical care, religious proselytisation, questionable finances; (b) Questions raised about conditions in her homes. Supporters counter: she served the DESTITUTE REJECTED even by hospitals; aim was COMFORT, not sophisticated care; financial transparency improved post-Nobel. PUBLISHED: No autobiography; her letters (posthumously, ‘Come Be My Light’, 2007) revealed she experienced decades of SPIRITUAL DARKNESS (‘dark night of the soul’) while outwardly smiling + serving — a testament to faith despite doubt. QUOTES: ‘NOT ALL OF US CAN DO GREAT THINGS. BUT WE CAN DO SMALL THINGS WITH GREAT LOVE’; ‘BE FAITHFUL IN SMALL THINGS BECAUSE IT IS IN THEM THAT YOUR STRENGTH LIES’. ‘for her work undertaken in the struggle to overcome poverty and distress, which also constitutes a threat to peace’; founded MISSIONARIES OF CHARITY (1950, Kolkata).

questions.stem: The SCIENTIST who has won the Nobel Prize in both PHYSICS and CHEMISTRY is:
questions.explanation: MARIE CURIE (1867-1934) — Polish-born French physicist-chemist; born MARIA SKŁODOWSKA in Warsaw. HOLDS UNIQUE RECORDS: (1) FIRST WOMAN to win a Nobel Prize; (2) ONLY PERSON to win Nobel Prizes in TWO DIFFERENT SCIENCES (Physics + Chemistry); (3) FIRST FAMILY with multiple Nobels (husband Pierre, daughter Irène Joliot-Curie + Frédéric Joliot-Curie also won). NOBEL 1 — PHYSICS 1903 (shared with husband PIERRE CURIE + HENRI BECQUEREL) ‘in recognition of the extraordinary services they have rendered by their joint researches on the RADIATION phenomena discovered by Professor Henri Becquerel’. The term ‘RADIOACTIVITY’ was coined by Marie Curie. NOBEL 2 — CHEMISTRY 1911 ‘in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements RADIUM and POLONIUM, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element’. POLONIUM (discovered 1898) — named after POLAND, her homeland (a patriotic statement: Poland was partitioned at the time, not independent). RADIUM (discovered 1898). Curies PROCESSED TONNES of PITCHBLENDE (uranium ore) from a Bohemian mine to isolate a few DECIGRAMS of radium — in a dilapidated shed, using buckets of chemicals + stirring with an iron rod, often with bare hands. Unaware of radiation hazards (science was new), both Curies suffered from long-term radiation exposure; Marie died of APLASTIC ANAEMIA from radiation 1934. Her laboratory notebooks are STILL radioactive today, kept in lead-lined boxes. PIERRE CURIE (1859-1906) — French physicist; also known for discovering PIEZOELECTRICITY with his brother Jacques. Died tragically in 1906: slipped on wet road in Paris + crushed by horse-drawn wagon, age 46. WWI CONTRIBUTION: Marie Curie designed MOBILE RADIOLOGICAL UNITS (‘PETITES CURIES’) — 20 units for battlefield X-ray imaging, saved thousands of Allied soldiers' lives; trained 150 women operators. CURIE FAMILY HEIRLOOM: 5 Nobel Prizes across 3 generations: Marie + Pierre (Physics 1903), Marie (Chemistry 1911), daughter IRÈNE JOLIOT-CURIE + son-in-law FRÉDÉRIC JOLIOT (Chemistry 1935 — artificial radioactivity), + Henry Labouisse (Marie's son-in-law/grandson-in-law, received Peace Nobel 1965 on behalf of UNICEF). RESEARCH INSTITUTIONS: INSTITUT CURIE, Paris — still a leading cancer research centre. OTHERS who won 2 Nobels in SCIENCE: (1) JOHN BARDEEN (Physics 1956 + 1972; transistor + superconductivity — BCS theory). (2) LINUS PAULING (Chemistry 1954 for chemical bonding + Peace 1962 for nuclear test ban — ONLY person with 2 UNSHARED Nobels in different categories). (3) FREDERICK SANGER (Chemistry 1958 + 1980; protein sequencing + DNA sequencing — Sanger sequencing). (4) KARL BARRY SHARPLESS (Chemistry 2001 + 2022; chirally catalysed + click chemistry). That's 5 individuals with 2 Nobels; only Curie did it across different science fields. ORGANISATIONS: ICRC (Red Cross) — 3 Peace Nobels (1917, 1944, 1963); UNHCR — 2 (1954, 1981). Physics 1903 (radioactivity, with husband Pierre + Henri Becquerel) and Chemistry 1911 (for discovery of polonium + radium); FIRST WOMAN + FIRST PERSON to win 2 Nobels in SCIENCE.

questions.stem: EINSTEIN won the NOBEL PRIZE IN PHYSICS 1921 for:

options.option_text: His services to THEORETICAL PHYSICS, especially for his DISCOVERY of the LAW OF THE PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT

questions.explanation: ALBERT EINSTEIN (1879-1955) — German-Swiss-American physicist; perhaps the most iconic scientist of the 20th century. NOBEL PRIZE IN PHYSICS 1921 (awarded in 1922, as 1921 was initially withheld) — citation: ‘for his services to theoretical physics, and especially for his discovery of the LAW OF THE PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT’. Notably, the award DID NOT explicitly cite the THEORY OF RELATIVITY — because at the time, relativity was still CONTROVERSIAL + not yet definitively verified (GTR's prediction of light bending by Sun was only confirmed in the 1919 eclipse expedition; some still doubted). The photoelectric effect result (1905) was by then well-established. PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT — emission of ELECTRONS from a metal surface when light is shone on it. Before Einstein, this was unexplained: (1) classical wave theory predicted that the ENERGY of ejected electrons should depend on light INTENSITY (brighter → more energy); experiments showed energy depends on FREQUENCY (colour), not intensity; (2) there was a THRESHOLD FREQUENCY below which NO electrons were emitted, regardless of how bright; (3) electrons were emitted INSTANTANEOUSLY when light hit, even at very low intensities. EINSTEIN'S EXPLANATION (1905): light is not a continuous wave but consists of discrete PACKETS (QUANTA) of energy, which he called LICHTQUANT (light quanta; later renamed PHOTONS by G.N. Lewis, 1926). Each photon carries energy E = hν (Planck's constant × frequency). An electron absorbs ONE photon; if hν ≥ work function (threshold energy) of the metal, electron is ejected with kinetic energy KE = hν − Φ. Einstein's equation beautifully explained all 3 puzzles. Built on PLANCK's 1900 quantum hypothesis (for black body radiation) but explicitly stated light ITSELF is quantised. Confirmed by ROBERT MILLIKAN's experiments 1914-16 (Millikan won Nobel 1923 partly for this, + oil-drop electron charge). IMPACT: this paper + the CURIE/RUTHERFORD/BOHR work founded QUANTUM MECHANICS. Einstein remained conflicted — his paper started quantum, yet he was UNCOMFORTABLE with quantum randomness; famous quote: ‘GOD DOES NOT PLAY DICE WITH THE UNIVERSE’. Debated Niels Bohr about interpretations for decades (Copenhagen interpretation vs Einstein's hidden-variables). Bell's theorem (1964) + Aspect's experiments (1982, Nobel 2022) eventually supported Bohr's side. EINSTEIN'S 1905 ‘MIRACLE YEAR’ (ANNUS MIRABILIS) — while a PATENT CLERK in Bern, age 26, Einstein published FOUR REVOLUTIONARY PAPERS: (1) Photoelectric effect — cited for Nobel; (2) BROWNIAN MOTION — confirmed atomic-molecular theory of matter, provided method to count atoms (Avogadro's number); (3) SPECIAL RELATIVITY — time dilation, length contraction, relativity of simultaneity; (4) Mass-energy equivalence E = mc². All in one year, all from a patent clerk's desk, in his spare time. 1915 — published GENERAL RELATIVITY (gravity = spacetime curvature); confirmed by 1919 eclipse (Eddington expedition) — instantly made Einstein a global celebrity. OTHER CONTRIBUTIONS: Bose-Einstein statistics (with Satyendra Nath Bose, Indian physicist); condensed matter; cosmological constant (‘biggest blunder’, now revived for dark energy); EPR paradox (quantum entanglement). Later life: EMIGRATED to USA 1933 after Nazi rise; joined Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton; 1939 letter to FDR led to Manhattan Project (though Einstein himself didn't work on bomb); post-war advocate of nuclear disarmament + world govt; declined offer to be 2nd President of Israel (1952). Died 1955, aged 76, Princeton. which established the quantum/particle nature of light (photons).

questions.stem: The NOBEL PRIZE CEREMONY is held annually on DEC 10 (Nobel's death anniversary) in which TWO cities?

options.option_text: STOCKHOLM (Sweden) for all prizes + OSLO (Norway) for the Peace Prize

questions.explanation: NOBEL PRIZE CEREMONIES held annually on 10 DECEMBER (anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, 1896) — IN TWO CITIES: (1) STOCKHOLM (Sweden) — for Physics, Chemistry, Physiology/Medicine, Literature, Economic Sciences (5 prizes); at STOCKHOLM CONCERT HALL (Konserthuset), followed by banquet at STOCKHOLM CITY HALL (Stadshuset) — 1,300 guests in the Blue Hall, served by servers in traditional livery. (2) OSLO (Norway) — for PEACE PRIZE only; at OSLO CITY HALL (Rådhus); attended by Norwegian Royal Family + PM + Storting. WHY TWO CITIES? At the time of Nobel's will (1895), Sweden and Norway were in a POLITICAL UNION (under the Swedish King, 1814-1905). Nobel specified that the PEACE PRIZE committee would be appointed by the NORWEGIAN STORTING (parliament), while the others by Swedish institutions — perhaps reflecting his belief that Norway was less militaristic + more peaceful, or perhaps to share the recognition across the union. After Norway's INDEPENDENCE in 1905, the arrangement continued, cementing this geographic split. FORMAL CEREMONY includes: (1) Laureates wear white tie + tails (men) or full-length evening gowns (women); (2) Presentation by Swedish/Norwegian Royal Family (currently King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden presents; Crown Prince Haakon of Norway for Peace); (3) Each laureate receives (a) a GOLD MEDAL (23-carat, weighs 175g, diameter 66 mm, depicting Nobel's profile on obverse with different scene on reverse for each prize), (b) a DIPLOMA (personalised artwork by Swedish artists), (c) a CASH AWARD. The CASH PRIZE (as of 2024): 11 million Swedish Kronor (~$1 million / ~₹8.3 crore) per prize category. If shared among multiple laureates, they split it. Not indexed to inflation routinely; adjusted by the Nobel Foundation based on returns on Nobel's bequest investments. Each laureate also delivers a NOBEL LECTURE (~45 min) in the days before/after the ceremony at a respective Swedish/Norwegian institution. Awards are ANNOUNCED in OCTOBER — typically Physiology/Medicine first (Monday), Physics (Tuesday), Chemistry (Wednesday), Literature (Thursday), Peace (Friday), Economic Sciences (next Monday). Announcements attract global media coverage. NOBEL FOUNDATION, Stockholm, manages the endowment (worth SEK ~5.5 billion in 2023). AWARDING INSTITUTIONS per will: (a) Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences — PHYSICS + CHEMISTRY + ECONOMIC SCIENCES (latter added 1968); (b) Karolinska Institute's Nobel Assembly — MEDICINE/PHYSIOLOGY; (c) Swedish Academy — LITERATURE; (d) Norwegian Nobel Committee (5 members appointed by Storting) — PEACE. NOMINATIONS: submitted by qualified persons (past laureates, professors, academy members, heads of state for Peace, etc.). Nomination process opens in Sept, closes Jan 31. NOMINATIONS kept SECRET for 50 YEARS. Candidate cannot nominate themselves. 2024 Nobel winners included: Peace to NIHON HIDANKYO; Physics to Hopfield+Hinton (AI); Chemistry to Baker+Hassabis+Jumper (AlphaFold+protein design); Medicine to Victor Ambros + Gary Ruvkun (microRNA); Literature to HAN KANG (first Korean woman); Economics to Daron Acemoglu + Simon Johnson + James Robinson (institutions + prosperity). a division specified in Alfred Nobel's will reflecting Sweden-Norway union at the time.

questions.stem: The YOUNGEST person ever to win a NOBEL PRIZE in any category is:

options.option_text: MALALA YOUSAFZAI — at age 17 years, 218 days, won NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 (shared with Kailash Satyarthi)

questions.explanation: MALALA YOUSAFZAI (b. 12 July 1997) — age 17 years, 218 days when awarded NOBEL PEACE PRIZE 2014 (jointly with Kailash Satyarthi, announced 10 Oct 2014; ceremony 10 Dec 2014, Oslo). YOUNGEST NOBEL LAUREATE EVER in any category. Previous record for youngest ANY category: (1) WILLIAM LAWRENCE BRAGG — won Physics Nobel 1915 at age 25 (jointly with his father W.H. Bragg, for X-ray crystallography of crystals — Bragg's law: nλ = 2d·sinθ). Youngest Physics laureate. (2) MAIRÉAD CORRIGAN — Peace Nobel 1976 at age 32 (Northern Ireland Peace). (3) TAWAKKOL KARMAN — Peace Nobel 2011 at age 32 (Yemeni activist, Arab Spring). Malala broke all these. YOUNGEST in other categories: (1) PHYSICS — Lawrence Bragg (25, 1915); (2) MEDICINE — Frederick Banting (32, 1923, insulin); (3) CHEMISTRY — Frédéric Joliot-Curie (35, 1935); (4) LITERATURE — RUDYARD KIPLING (41, 1907 — author of ‘Jungle Book’, ‘Kim’; Indian-born Englishman, first English-language laureate); (5) ECONOMIC SCIENCES — Esther Duflo (46, 2019 — second woman to win Economics Nobel, French-American, wife of Abhijit Banerjee); (6) PEACE — Malala (17, 2014). OLDEST NOBEL LAUREATE: JOHN GOODENOUGH — Chemistry 2019 at age 97 (lithium-ion battery), shared with Stanley Whittingham + Akira Yoshino. Goodenough died 2023 at 100. Before him: LEONID HURWICZ (Economics 2007, at 90). ARTHUR ASHKIN (Physics 2018, at 96, optical tweezers). DORIS LESSING (Literature 2007, at 88). OLDEST Physics: John B. Goodenough. HIGHLIGHTED RECORDS in Nobel history: (a) MOST NOBELS in one family: CURIE FAMILY (5 Nobels) — Marie (Physics 1903 + Chemistry 1911), Pierre (Physics 1903), Irène Joliot-Curie (Chemistry 1935 with husband Frédéric Joliot). (b) FATHER-SON: Lawrence Bragg + Henry Bragg (Physics 1915); Niels Bohr (Physics 1922) + Aage Bohr (Physics 1975); Hans von Euler-Chelpin (Chemistry 1929) + Ulf von Euler (Medicine 1970); Manne Siegbahn (Physics 1924) + Kai Siegbahn (Physics 1981); Arthur Kornberg (Medicine 1959) + Roger Kornberg (Chemistry 2006). (c) HUSBAND-WIFE: Marie + Pierre Curie, Gerty + Carl Cori (Medicine 1947), Irène + Frédéric Joliot-Curie, May-Britt + Edvard Moser (Medicine 2014 — spatial navigation), Esther Duflo + Abhijit Banerjee (Economics 2019). (d) POSTHUMOUS: Dag Hammarskjöld (Peace 1961, UN Secretary-General killed in plane crash), Erik Axel Karlfeldt (Literature 1931), Ralph Steinman (Medicine 2011 — died 3 days before). Since 1974, rule changed: no new posthumous awards EXCEPT if laureate dies between announcement + ceremony. (e) REFUSED: JEAN-PAUL SARTRE (Literature 1964, declined — disliked official honours), LE DUC THO (Peace 1973, declined — Vietnam War ongoing). (f) HITLER's Germany forced 3 German laureates to refuse in the 1930s. (g) NO PRIZE awarded during WWI + WWII for some categories. (h) ORGANISATIONS that won Peace: ICRC (3x), UNHCR (2x), IAEA (2005), IPCC (2007, with Al Gore), OPCW (2013), EU (2012). (i) Prize CAN BE SHARED by up to 3 individuals or organizations.
